readerTitle: Why the agency with the better work lost the client
caseNote: 가상 사례 (디자인 에이전시, 제조사 사내 법무팀) + 실제 연구 (SERVQUAL, Parasuraman·Zeithaml·Berry)
insight: 고객은 평균이 아니라 최악의 경우에 맞춰 행동한다. 그래서 가끔 뛰어난 서비스보다 매번 믿을 수 있는 서비스가 더 가치 있다.
misconception: 평균 품질이 높거나 가끔 고객을 감동시키면 고객 경험은 좋아진다.

sources.text: Parasuraman, A., Zeithaml, V. A., & Berry, L. L. (1988). SERVQUAL: A multiple-item scale for measuring consumer perceptions of service quality. Journal of Retailing, 64(1).
Zeithaml, V. A., Parasuraman, A., & Berry, L. L. (1990). Delivering Quality Service. Free Press.
에이전시와 사내 법무팀 사례, 차트 점수는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: SERVQUAL 연구에서 고객이 다섯 차원(신뢰성, 반응성, 확신성, 공감성, 유형성) 중 신뢰성(reliability)을 가장 중요하게 꼽았다는 내용을 Zeithaml·Parasuraman·Berry(1990) 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치 없이 '가장 중요하게 평가했다'고만 적었습니다.
softwareNote의 '항상 2초 로딩이 가끔 10초 멈추는 1초 로딩보다 낫게 느껴질 수 있다'는 일반적 설명이며 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 출처를 확인하세요.

cards.title: The agency with the better work lost the client.
body: Two design agencies worked for the same retail brand for six months. One produced the best campaign the brand had ever run. It also missed two deadlines.
The other agency was never brilliant. It was simply good, every single time. At renewal, the brand kept the second one.

image.label: Two agency desks, one with a trophy and a late stamp, one with a neat stack of files
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽 책상에는 반짝이는 트로피와 'LATE' 도장이 찍힌 서류, 오른쪽 책상에는 가지런히 쌓인 서류 더미와 체크 표시. 오른쪽에 고객이 계약서를 건네는 모습. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: One improvement, one budget.
body: You run a small marketing agency. Most client deliveries are strong, and some are outstanding. But about one in five arrives late or needs heavy fixes.
You can afford one improvement this year. Which do you choose?

options.text: Hire a star creative to make your best work even better
options.feedback: Higher peaks help you win pitches. But clients burned by a late delivery still have to check everything you send.

options.text: Build checklists and review steps so every delivery meets the same standard
options.feedback: You spend less time on showpiece work. In return, clients can stop double-checking you, and that is what keeps them renewing.

options.text: Send surprise extras to your biggest clients
options.feedback: Delight feels good, but a gift doesn't cancel a missed deadline. Clients remember the delivery that caused them trouble.

cards.title: Higher average, lower trust.
body: The brand's marketing lead scored each month's work out of 10.
cards.callout: Agency A averaged **8.0**. Agency B averaged 7.7. The brand still chose B.

cards.title: Consistency
body: **Consistency** means customers get the same level of service every time, so they can predict what comes next.

Customers don't act on your average. They act on your worst case. After Agency A's bad months, the marketing lead checked every file, padded every deadline and kept a backup freelancer on call. That extra work is a real cost, and the customer pays it.

image.label: Two targets: scattered hits near the center versus a tight cluster
image.brief: 과녁 두 개 나란히. 왼쪽 과녁은 정중앙 근처에 몇 발, 가장자리에 몇 발이 흩어져 있고 'Agency A' 라벨. 오른쪽 과녁은 중앙 바로 옆에 촘촘하게 모인 탄착군과 'Agency B' 라벨. 오른쪽이 더 믿음직해 보이도록.

cards.title: Reliability tops the list.
body: In the 1980s, researchers Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry studied how customers judge service. Their model, SERVQUAL, grouped it into five areas: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and physical surroundings.
Across their studies, customers rated **reliability** as the most important: doing what you promised, dependably and accurately.
Friendliness and polish help. They rarely make up for being undependable.

cards.title: People pay for no bad surprises.
body: A traveler will often pick a familiar chain over a local restaurant that might be better. They aren't buying the best meal. They're buying a meal with no bad surprise.
The same logic explains kitchen checklists, call-center guides and standard report formats. Each one shrinks the gap between your best day and your worst.
cards.softwareNote: Users notice uneven performance more than slow performance. An app that always loads in two seconds can feel better than one that usually loads in one and sometimes hangs for ten.

cards.title: Consistent isn't the same as rigid.
body: Consistency is about results customers can count on, not identical scripts. A rule followed even when it clearly fails a customer feels consistent to you and careless to them.
And consistently mediocre is still mediocre. Set the floor high enough first, then make it dependable. Checklists, training and reviews take time, so spend it where customers depend on you most.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead the legal team at a manufacturer. Sales sends you contracts to review. Some come back in a day, others take two weeks, and nobody knows which it will be.
Some sales reps now skip the review or quietly use outside lawyers. What do you do?

options.text: Promise five working days for standard contracts, and quote a date for complex ones
options.feedback: You lose a few one-day wins. But sales can plan around you again, and going around your team stops being worth it.

options.text: Hire another lawyer to clear the backlog faster
options.feedback: A faster average helps. But if reps still can't tell when a contract will be done, they still can't plan.

options.text: Let reps flag urgent contracts for same-day review
options.feedback: Soon every contract is urgent, and the rest wait even longer. The gap between best and worst gets wider, not narrower.

cards.title: Customers plan around your worst day, not your best.
body: Dependable service lets customers stop checking, padding and preparing for trouble. That relief is worth more than an occasional wow.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you deliver often. Write down your best and worst recent example. Work on narrowing that gap before raising the peak.
